claims.text: The target as-cast Mg-containing alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
The as-cast alloy contains a heterogeneous mixture of metastable solid-solution domains and intermetallic compounds.
Thermal exposure transforms metastable Mg-rich solid-solution regions into stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Thermal exposure increases the volume fraction of stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Thermal aging partitions Mg out of metastable solid-solution regions and into stable intermetallic phases.
Phase evolution produces Mg segregation at the alloy surface.
Mg redistribution changes the elemental composition of the surface and its oxide scale during oxidation.
Changes in surface-film or oxide-scale composition can modify corrosion resistance.
Changes in oxide-scale adhesion and defect density modify corrosion resistance.
Changes in oxide-scale adhesion and defect density modify high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
Thermally aged specimens will have a measurably different surface oxide composition than as-cast specimens.
Thermally aged specimens will exhibit altered corrosion current density relative to the as-cast baseline.
Thermally aged specimens will exhibit an altered high-temperature oxidation rate relative to the as-cast baseline.
The as-cast baseline has an initial oxide-scale behavior established during fabrication.
Transformation kinetics and the extent of Mg segregation depend on alloy composition and thermal-exposure parameters.

contradictions.description: The causal hypothesis identifies thermal exposure as the driver of phase transformation, but the intervention and falsification design allow corrosive exposure alone through 'and/or' language, including salt spray or aqueous media that need not provide thermal aging. Such a comparison would not necessarily test the asserted thermal driver.
